world.setting: Contemporary United States: Graceland in Memphis, a grey winter cabin in Provincetown on Cape Cod, Silicon Valley tech campuses, and university labs at Harvard, MIT and UC Irvine

signatureObjects.name: The Skinner Box
signatureObjects.why: The bare laboratory box with a lever the pigeon pecks for pellets — the episode's recurring image of variable-reward feeds that never let the brain move on

signatureObjects.name: The Slot Machine
signatureObjects.why: The casino machine with spinning reels and a lever — the episode's recurring image of feeds tuned against your psychology by thousands of engineers

cabin.look: A lonely wooden cabin on the grey winter shore of Provincetown, low waves dragging, a pale vast ocean under a flat cold sky.

office.look: A fluorescent open-plan office where Slack pings, emails chime and colleagues tap shoulders every few minutes of every hour.

desk.look: A cluttered home workstation at night: laptop glow, an important half-written email, a phone buzzing beside it.

street.look: An ordinary town street where a relaxed man walks, bored and thoughtless, toward a waiting bus.

forest.look: A deep shadowed forest where a deer freezes mid-step, nostrils wide, listening for a predator it cannot see.

bedroom.look: A dark bedroom at 2 a.m., blue phone-light on a sleepless face, hours bleeding away in a glowing scroll.

sleepLab.look: The Harvard sleep lab: a white observation room, electrode caps, monitoring screens tracing exhausted brains.

bookshop.look: A beloved bookshop sanctuary smelling of paper, tall wooden shelves, a young bookseller behind the counter.

graceland.look: The Jungle Room at Graceland: green shag carpet, carved tiki furniture, waterfall wall — Elvis's favorite hideout.

objects.why: The buzzing leash: texts interrupting emails, Graceland iPads, Snapchat hidden under a jacket.
The river of attention itself; the switching tax is a toll booth in its middle, and tech bottles it back as likes and ads.
The episode's image of variable-reward feeds: a pigeon pecking a lever, never given the signal to move on.
The episode's image of hijack design: a machine tuned against your psychology by thousands of engineers.
The chapter Johann cannot finish in Provincetown; deep reading as an atrophying skill.
Exhausted time: the sleep lab, sleepless scrolling, the twenty-minute refocus cost of every glance away.
Flow's sweet spot where challenge meets skill — boredom on one side, anxiety on the other.
The big ideas born in mind-wandering and boredom, starved by constant stimulation.
The shackles of the switching tax and hijack design — and breaking them through collective refusal.
The boardroom engineers pulling attention strings from a thousand miles away.
Surveillance advertising that targets, tracks and sells each glance back to you.
The closing confrontation: are you freely choosing to look, or was this moment engineered?
The important half-written email that a single buzz disassembles into restarted neural machines.
The single drop extracted: likes, notifications and targeted ads sold back glass by glass.

spine.claim: Johann ditches his phone for three months in a Provincetown cabin and still cannot finish a chapter: the damage is not the device, it is the system that rewired his brain.
Interlocking forces — the switching tax, murdered flow, exhaustion, skimming brains, starved wandering — levy a toll on every attempt to think deeply.
Underneath sits a machine: surveillance capitalism runs Skinner-box schedules and slot-machine feeds, tuned by thousands of engineers against your own intentions.
The bill lands in the body — sleeplessness, stress, the deer-in-the-forest precarity brain — and individual life-hacks are exposed as cruel optimism.
Stolen things can be taken back: ban the business model, shorten the working week, free children's play — refuse together to hand attention over.
